title: Muons Shouldn't Reach the Ground. They Do.
description:
What Happens If You Travel Near Light Speed?
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rVqgtkBV3jc

Cosmic rays strike the upper atmosphere and create muons that live for only about two millionths of a second — barely 600 metres of flight at classical speeds. Travelling near the speed of light, relativistic time dilation slows their internal clocks so they survive the journey and reach the ground.

Sources: Frisch & Smith 1963 (American Journal of Physics 31, 342–355), muon relativistic time dilation measured from Mount Washington to sea level (https://doi.org/10.1119/1.1969508) · Particle Data Group, Workman et al. 2022 (PTEP 2022, 083C01), cosmic-ray muon mean lifetime (~2.2 microseconds) and sea-level flux (~1 per cm² per minute) · Taylor & Wheeler 1992 (Spacetime Physics, 2nd ed.), Ch. 3, relativistic proper time and the Lorentz factor.

Pictures: NASA International Space Station Earth observations (Earth Views from the International Space Station and NHQ_2019_0626 Earth Views from the ISS) alongside custom code graphics and AI-assisted voice and editing. Facts: every number is checked against the sources listed above.
Image credits: Images and visualisations courtesy of NASA. Use does not imply endorsement. Earth Views from the International Space Station: NASA; Earth Views from the ISS (NHQ_2019_0626): NASA.
